propositions.text: If returned to Turkey, he will be persecuted for political opinion and religion.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) claims that if returned to Turkey, his country of nationality, he will be persecuted based on his political opinion (membership in the HDP (People's Democratic Party)) and his religion (Alevi Muslim).

propositions.text: RPD refused refugee protection claim on July 14, 2017 for lack of credibility and exclusion under Article 1E due to permanent residence in Germany.
propositions.quote: His claim for refugee protection was refused by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) on July 14, 2017 based on a finding that he lacked credibility and was excluded under Article 1E of the Geneva Convention,1 as he was a permanent resident of Germany.

propositions.text: He appeals to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).
propositions.quote: He now appeals to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).

paragraphs.summary: The applicant claims persecution if returned to Turkey; the RPD refused protection for lack of credibility and exclusion; he appeals to the RAD.

propositions.text: Confirms RPD decision that appellant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection; appeal dismissed.
propositions.quote: I confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The appeal is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court confirms the RPD decision and dismisses the appeal.

propositions.text: Claims membership in Kurdish party (HDP) and Alevi organizations; detained, interrogated, tortured in Turkey.
propositions.quote: The Appellant claims to be a member of the "Kurdish party (HDP) and Alevi organizations (Pir Sultan Abdal association)." As a result of his political activities, he claims that he was detained, interrogated and tortured by the Turkish authorities.

propositions.text: Applied for Canadian visa via agent/smuggler, claiming residence and employment in Germany.
propositions.quote: Through the use of an agent/smuggler,2 the Appellant applied for a Canadian visa, which was issued on XXXX XXXX, 2016. In support of the visa application, his agent/smuggler claimed that the Appellant resided in Germany and worked for a German company.

propositions.text: Submitted passport, German residency card, banking documents, and employment letter for visa application.
propositions.quote: A number of documents were submitted, including the Appellant's passport, a German Residency card (said to have been issued by the authorities in XXXX, Germany), banking documents indicating that the Appellant resided in Berlin and a letter from a German company confirming the Appellant's employment.

propositions.text: Arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017 and made inland refugee claim on March 27, 2017.
propositions.quote: The Appellant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017. He made an inland claim for refugee status on March 27, 2017.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant claims political and religious membership, was detained in Turkey, applied for Canadian visa with documents claiming German residence, arrived in Canada, and claimed refugee status.

propositions.text: Requests admission of two new documents: German Consulate letter denying registration and affidavit from friend about political activities.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has requested the admission of two documents at appeal: i) a letter from the German Consulate in Toronto indicating that the authorities in XXXX "confirmed that there is no registration of a person named XXXX XXXX XXXX, DOB: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Citizenship; TURKEY" and ii) an affidavit from a friend of the Appellant, a Mr. XXXX, dated September 25, 2017, outlining the Appellant's political activities in Turkey and in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant requests admission of a German Consulate letter denying registration and an affidavit from a friend about political activities.

propositions.text: Subsection 110(4) IRPA limits new evidence admission to evidence arising after RPD rejection, not reasonably available then, or not reasonably expected to be presented then.
propositions.quote: Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA limits the admission of evidence in an appeal before the RAD to evidence that: 1) arose after the RPD's rejection of the claim; 2) was not reasonably available at the time of the RPD's rejection of the claim; or 3) an Appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of the RPD's rejection of the claim.

propositions.text: RAD rule 3(3)(g)(iii) requires detailed submissions on how new evidence meets subsection 110(4) and relates to appellant.
propositions.quote: RAD rule 3(3)(g)(iii) provides that an Appellant seeking the admission of new evidence must provide full and detailed submissions regarding how the evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) and how that evidence relates to the Appellant.

propositions.text: If new evidence admissible under 110(4), must consider Singh factors: newness, credibility, relevance.
propositions.quote: If I find that the new evidence is admissible under subsection 110(4), I must then consider whether the evidence meets the factors elaborated by the Federal Court of Appeal in the Singh case, i.e. newness, credibility and relevance.

propositions.text: Threshold for admitting new evidence before RAD is high.
propositions.quote: The threshold for the admission of new evidence before the RAD is high.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the legal test for admitting new evidence on appeal, including subsection 110(4) IRPA and Singh factors.

propositions.text: Does not explain why German Consulate letter was not obtained before RPD rejection.
propositions.quote: As to the letter from the German Consulate, the Appellant does not offer an explanation as to why he could not have obtained this letter before the RPD's rejection of his claim.

propositions.text: Affidavit notes document requested August 4, 2017; legal memo states evidence not present at RPD hearing.
propositions.quote: An affidavit in support of the request for the admission of the document merely notes that the document was requested on August 4, 2017 and the Appellant's Legal Memorandum states that the "piece of evidence was not present at the time of the hearing before the RPD".

propositions.text: No argument why German Consulate document was not sought earlier or was not reasonably available or expected at RPD rejection.
propositions.quote: No argument is made as to why the information from the German Consulate was not sought until after the rejection of the claim. Nor does the Appellant indicate why the document was not reasonably available or could not reasonably have been expected to be presented at the time of the RPD's rejection of the claim.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant offers no explanation why the German Consulate letter was not obtained or presented before the RPD rejection.

propositions.text: Normally would not argue for appellant, but fairness requires examining background of issue.
propositions.quote: Normally, my consideration of the matter would end here: it does not fall to me to make an argument for an Appellant where none has been made by him or his counsel. However, in the circumstances, I feel that fairness requires me to look at the background of the issue.

propositions.text: Hearing adjourned to allow Ministry to get signed permission to contact German authorities for Article 1E exclusion.
propositions.quote: The hearing was originally scheduled for May 29, 2017, but was adjourned in order to ensure that the Ministry-which had earlier requested permission from the Appellant to contact the German authorities in relation to a possible Article 1E exclusion-received the signed permission document from the Appellant.

propositions.text: Hearing resumed July 29, 2017; Ministry declined to intervene despite earlier request.
propositions.quote: The hearing resumed on July 29, 2017; however the Ministry-despite its earlier request-declined to intervene.

propositions.text: Because Ministry initially sought German contact, it was reasonable for appellant not to seek letter earlier; appellant could not reasonably have been expected to present letter at RPD rejection.
propositions.quote: Because of the Ministry's initial interest in contacting the German authorities, it was reasonable, I find, for the Appellant not to have done so. As such, I find that the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented the letter from the German consulate at the time of the RPD's rejection of the claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds fairness requires examining background; Ministry's initial interest justified appellant's delay in obtaining German Consulate letter; letter admissible under 110(4).

propositions.text: German Consulate letter is credible, new, relevant, and admissible.
propositions.quote: Based on my examination of the document, I can see no basis to find that it is lacking in credibility. It is on letterhead, is signed and appears official. It is clearly new information and it is highly relevant to an essential finding of the RPD: that the Appellant had permanent residency in Germany. Consequently, I find the document admissible.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the German Consulate letter credible, new, relevant, and admissible.

propositions.text: Offers no argument how affidavit from Mr. XXXX complies with subsection 110(4).
propositions.quote: Once again, the Appellant offers no argument as to how the affidavit from Mr. XXXX XXXX sworn September 25, 2017, complies with subsection 110(4).

propositions.text: Affidavit contains no information that could not have been provided to RPD before claim rejection; affidavit inadmissible.
propositions.quote: It is clear from its content, that it contains no information that could not have been either provided to the RPD at the time of the Appellant's hearing or during the period after the last session of the hearing (June 29, 2017) and before the Appellant's claim was rejected (July 14, 2017). As such, I find it inadmissible.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant offers no argument for affidavit's compliance with subsection 110(4); court finds affidavit inadmissible as information was available before claim rejection.

propositions.text: Requests hearing before RAD under section 110(6) IRPA due to new evidence and RPD not addressing credibility.
propositions.quote: The Appellant is asking to have hearing [sic] before the RAD pursuant to section 110(6) of the IRPA. The RPD did not address issue credibility [sic] as it solely based its decision on exclusion under Article 1A [sic]. There is also new evidence by of Affidavit from Mr. XXXX. The RAD may wish to hear evidence from Mr. XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant requests a hearing before RAD under section 110(6) IRPA due to new evidence and RPD's failure to address credibility.

propositions.text: Subsection 110(3) IRPA requires RAD to proceed without hearing unless subsection 110(6) conditions met for new evidence.
propositions.quote: The principle under subsection 110(3) of the IRPA that the RAD must proceed without a hearing, is subject to an exception, elaborated in subsection 110(6).

propositions.text: Section 110(6) allows hearing if new evidence raises serious credibility issue, is central to decision, and if accepted justifies allowing or rejecting claim.
propositions.quote: The latter subsection provides a hearing may be held where three conditions in relation to the new evidence are met. The new evidence must: a) raise a serious issue with respect to the Appellant's credibility; b) be central to the decision with respect to his refugee protection claim and c) if accepted, justify allowing or rejecting his claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that RAD must proceed without hearing unless new evidence meets three conditions under subsection 110(6).

propositions.text: Affidavit inadmissible, so no need to consider subsection 110(6) conditions for it.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's justification for his request for a hearing centres primarily on the affidavit of Mr. XXXX; given my finding above that his affidavit is inadmissible, I need not have regard to the existence of the three conditions outlined in subsection 110(6) in relation to that affidavit.

propositions.text: Letter from German Consulate admitted but does not justify allowing or rejecting claim under section 110(6).
propositions.quote: As to the letter from the German Consulate, I find that the test at section 110(6) is not met: the evidence, though admitted, does not "justify allowing or rejecting his claim."

propositions.text: Letter impacts RPD's Article 1E exclusion finding but does not resolve credibility issue.
propositions.quote: The evidence certainly impacts on the RPD's finding-discussed below-that the Appellant's residence permit in Germany excludes him based on Article 1E; however that alone does not justify allowing or rejecting the Appellant's claim. The issue of his credibility remains.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds affidavit inadmissible and German Consulate letter insufficient to justify a hearing under section 110(6).

propositions.text: Whether appellant is disqualified under Article 1E due to German residency and credibility are determinative issues.
propositions.quote: The determinative issues in this case are i) whether the Appellant is disqualified from refugee protection in Canada under Article 1E of the Geneva Convention by virtue of having been recognized as a resident of Germany and ii) credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies German residency under Article 1E and credibility as the determinative issues.

propositions.text: Standard of review is correctness except where RPD has advantage assessing oral testimony, then reasonableness applies.
propositions.quote: The standard of review is correctness,7 except where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in the assessment of the oral testimony. If such an advantage exists, I will apply a standard of reasonableness.8 Where I do so, I will so indicate.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review is correctness unless RPD has advantage assessing oral testimony, then reasonableness applies.

propositions.text: RPD found on balance of probabilities that appellant had permanent residence in Germany and lacked credibility due to falsified passport.
propositions.quote: The RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant had permanent residence in Germany. It also found that the Appellant lacked credibly as he had submitted a falsified passport when making his refugee claim.

propositions.text: Argues he was not a resident of Germany and RPD erred in finding lack of credibility.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that he was not a resident of Germany and that the RPD's finding that he lacked credibility was in error.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found German residency and lack of credibility; the appellant argues both findings were erroneous.

propositions.text: RPD found Canadian visa officials accepted documents as authentic and appellant had permanent residency in Germany.
propositions.quote: The RPD, noting that the Canadian visa officials had accepted the documents submitted in support of the Appellant's visa application, found that they were, on a balance of probabilities, authentic and found further that he had, as indicated in the visa application, permanent residency in Germany.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found visa officials accepted documents as authentic and appellant had permanent residency in Germany.

propositions.text: Argues documents except passport were forgeries and RPD erred in assuming visa officials determined genuineness.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that all of the documents that were a part of his Canadian visa application, other than his passport, were forgeries. He argues that the RPD erred in finding that the Canadian officials who reviewed the visa application would have made a determination that the documentation was genuine; there was no evidence to this effect.

propositions.text: Argues visa officers may have been fooled by sophisticated forgeries, not genuine documents.
propositions.quote: Simply because the documentation was realistic enough to fool the visa officials did not mean that it was genuine. He notes that "it is quite likely that, when came [sic] across such documents that are forget [sic] sophisticatedly, the Visa officer may take them as genuine."

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues documents were forgeries and visa officials may have been fooled, so RPD erred in finding genuineness.

propositions.text: Admitted German Consulate letter is authentic and undermines RPD's finding of permanent residency in Germany.
propositions.quote: As noted, I have admitted into evidence the letter from the German Consulate indicating that the residency card was not valid and I can see no indication that that letter is anything other than authentic. As such, an important aspect of the RPD's finding that the Appellant had permanent residency in Germany is missing and I must review its finding on this point.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the German Consulate letter authentic and undermining the RPD's finding of German permanent residency.

propositions.text: Other visa application documents not found invalid, but invalid residency card means appellant was not German resident.
propositions.quote: Even though I have no reason to find that the other documents submitted as part of the Appellant's visa application were invalid, because the Residency Card is not valid, I do not share the RPD's conclusion that the Appellant was a German resident.

propositions.text: Finds on balance of probabilities appellant did not have permanent residency in Germany and RPD erred in Article 1E exclusion finding.
propositions.quote: I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant did not have permanent residency in Germany and that the RPD erred in finding that he was excluded from refugee protection by virtue of Article 1E.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant did not have German permanent residency and that RPD erred in Article 1E exclusion.

propositions.text: RPD found two versions of appellant's passport; second version had pages from different passport, undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: The RPD reviewed the Appellant's passport and found that there were two versions. In the version that was submitted to the Canadian officials in late 2016 in support of the Appellant's visa application, all pages appeared to be from the same passport and there was evidence of extensive travel on the part of the Appellant. In the second version, the one submitted as part of the Appellant's refugee claim in late March 2017, certain of the passport's pages-in particular the pages that, in the version submitted to the Canadian visa officials, featured stamps showing extensive travel-featured numbers that indicated that they were from a different passport.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found two versions of the appellant's passport, with the second version undermining credibility.

propositions.text: RPD suggested two passport versions exist because the real passport was modified to hide German connections
propositions.quote: The RPD suggested that the most likely explanation for the existence of two versions of the passport was that the Appellant's real passport was used in the application for a Canadian visa but that after the passport had been returned to the Appellant (with the Canadian visa in it), it had been modified in such a way that the Appellant's connections with Germany would be hidden

propositions.text: Appellant denied knowledge of fraud and blamed agent/smuggler
propositions.quote: When confronted with this, the Appellant denied all knowledge attributed any fraud to his agent/smuggler

propositions.text: RPD rejected Appellant's explanation and found Canadian officials would have noticed tampering
propositions.quote: The RPD rejected this explanation. As discussed above, it noted that that the Canadian officials would have examined the passport as part of the visa application process; had it been tampered with at the time of their examination, the officials would not have issued the visa.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found two passport versions because the real one was modified to hide German ties; the Appellant denied fraud, blaming smugglers; RPD rejected this.

propositions.text: Appellant claims he provided valid passport but never travelled outside Turkey
propositions.quote: The Appellant claims that he provided a valid passport to the agent/smuggler. However, at the same time, he claims that he had never travelled outside Turkey until he came to Canada.

propositions.text: Appellant argues RPD erred in assuming Canadian official verified genuineness of documents
propositions.quote: the Appellant argues that the RPD erred in finding that the Canadian official who reviewed the visa application would have made a determination that the documentation was genuine; simply because the documentation was realistic enough to fool the visa official, did not mean that it was genuine.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant claims he gave a valid passport but never left Turkey and argues the RPD erred in assuming Canadian officials verified document genuineness.

propositions.text: Examined two passport versions and confirmed they differ in passport numbers on pages
propositions.quote: I have closely examined the two versions of the Appellant's passport-the version that was submitted to Canadian visa officials and one that was submitted to as part of the Appellant's refugee claim-and confirm that the RPD was correct in finding that they were different.

propositions.text: Passport number XXXX appears on front cover and photo page in both versions
propositions.quote: With both versions the passport number is given on the front cover and on the photograph page (page 2) as XXXX.

propositions.text: Visa application passport has consistent passport number XXXX on all pages
propositions.quote: the version of the passport that was submitted as part of the application for the Canadian visa has the same passport number, XXXX, stamped on all of the pages provided

propositions.text: Refugee claim passport has inconsistent passport numbers on pages, some XXXX, some XXXX
propositions.quote: the version that was submitted as part of the Appellant's refugee claim does not. In the latter version of the passport, pages 1 (the cover) - 3 show the number XXXX; however, on pages 4 - 12 the passport number stamped on the document pages is XXXX.

propositions.text: Some pages have illegible numbers but some end with XXXX or XXXX; visa page linked to XXXX
propositions.quote: The numbers on most other pages are not entirely legible, however it is clear that pages 22 and 23 are stamped with a passport number ending in "XXXX"-presumably XXXX-and pages 52 and 53 are stamped with a number ending in "XXXX"-presumably XXXX. The Canadian visa, found at page 20, is linked to passport number XXXX; the passport number stamped on that page is not legible.

paragraphs.summary: The court examined both passports and confirmed differences in passport numbers on pages between visa and refugee claim versions.

propositions.text: Finds on balance of probabilities that passport submitted to Canadian visa officials was authentic
propositions.quote: I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the passport submitted to the Canadian visa officials was authentic.

propositions.text: Canadian visa officials would have noticed a clumsily modified passport
propositions.quote: Had the clumsily modified version been submitted to the visa officials, they would, on a balance of probabilities, have noticed. After all, their role is to ensure that applications for visas are legitimate.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the passport submitted to Canadian visa officials authentic and that officials would have noticed clumsy modifications.

propositions.text: Version submitted with refugee claim had substituted pages to hide travel evidence
propositions.quote: It is clear that the version submitted in support of the Appellant's refugee claim had substituted pages that corresponded with those pages in the passport submitted as part of the visa application where there was evidence of travel (pages 6 - 12).

propositions.text: Finds on balance of probabilities that there was an attempt to fraudulently modify the passport to hide travel stamps
propositions.quote: Consequently, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that there was an attempt to fraudulently modify the passport so that the travel stamps would not appear in the modified version.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the refugee claim passport had substituted pages to hide travel stamps, indicating fraudulent modification.

propositions.text: Appellant says he gave valid passport to agent/smuggler who modified it
propositions.quote: it is the position of the Appellant that he gave the agent/smuggler his valid passport and that any substitution of pages was the work of the agent/smuggler.

propositions.text: Agent/smuggler would have had to modify passport twice, including after visa officials returned it
propositions.quote: the agent/smuggler would have not only had to modify the passport with sufficient sophistication to fool Canadian visa officials, he would have also had to replace the pages containing the stamps after it was returned to the agent/smuggler from the Canadian visa officials but before the agent/smuggler returned it to the Appellant.

propositions.text: Such a passport would have pages from two different passports when Appellant entered Canada
propositions.quote: Such a scenario would mean that the Appellant would have entered Canada on a passport that featured pages stamped as being from two different passports.

propositions.text: This is implausible and illogical given CBSA's role and no advantage to agent/smuggler
propositions.quote: This is not only implausible-given that Canadian Border Security Agency (CBSA) officials are charged with ensuring that people entering Canada do so lawfully-it is also illogical: there would be no advantage to the agent/smuggler modifying the passport before the Appellant travelled and considerable disadvantage.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant claims agent modified passport; court finds this would require implausible double modification and is illogical given CBSA role.

propositions.text: Implausible that CBSA officials would not have spotted clumsily doctored passport at entry
propositions.quote: I am of the view that it is implausible that a passport, doctored in the rather clumsy way described, would not have been spotted by the CBSA officials if it had been was presented at Pearson Airport on XXXX XXXX, 2017.

propositions.text: Finds on balance of probabilities that Appellant travelled to Canada on unaltered passport
propositions.quote: Consequently, I find on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant travelled to Canada on his unaltered passport.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it implausible CBSA missed clumsy passport alterations and concludes Appellant travelled on unaltered passport.

propositions.text: Concludes passport was tampered with by Appellant after arrival and before refugee claim
propositions.quote: I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the passport was tampered with by the Appellant (or under his direction) sometime after the Appellant's arrival in Canada and before he surrendered it as part of his refugee claim.

propositions.text: Appellant may have removed travel evidence to strengthen refugee claim
propositions.quote: he may have thought that removing evidence of foreign travel would strengthen his refugee claim-perhaps by eliminating any risk that he would be faulted for not having made a claim in one of the countries to which he had travelled.

propositions.text: This act of fraud seriously undermines Appellant's credibility
propositions.quote: I find that this act of fraud seriously undermines the Appellant's credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant tampered with passport after arrival to hide travel, seriously undermining his credibility.

propositions.text: Finds travel stamps showing extensive travel including Germany are valid
propositions.quote: I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the travel stamps-which show extensive travel, including to Germany-are valid

propositions.text: Finds Appellant's testimony denying travel outside Germany was fabricated
propositions.quote: his testimony that he had never set foot outside Germany until he came to Canada was a fabrication.

propositions.text: This fabrication seriously undermines Appellant's credibility
propositions.quote: I find that this fabrication seriously undermines his credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds travel stamps valid and Appellant's denial of travel fabricated, seriously undermining credibility.

propositions.text: Before final credibility finding, court considers supporting documents provided to RPD
propositions.quote: before making a final finding regarding the Appellant's credibility, I turn to the supporting documents provided to the RPD.

propositions.text: Appellant submitted Turkish identity card matching name and birth date on passports
propositions.quote: the Appellant has submitted a Turkish identity card showing him to have the same name and date of birth as the person in each version of the passport.

propositions.text: Other documents include receipts for HDP membership fees, Pir Sultan Abdal Cultural Association membership and letter from Canadian Alevi Culture Centre
propositions.quote: The only other documents provided by the Appellant are receipts for the payment of membership fees to the HDP, receipts for the payment of membership fees to the Pir Sultan Abdal Cultural Association, a membership card from the Pir Sultan Abdal Cultural Association, a letter from the Canadian Alevi Culture Centre and photographs said to be of the Appellant.

paragraphs.summary: The court reviews supporting documents including identity card, membership receipts, letter, and photographs before final credibility finding.

propositions.text: Receipts for HDP membership fees appear valid and support Appellant's claim of membership
propositions.quote: The receipts for payment of membership fees to the HDP appear valid on their face and pertain to two years during which the Appellant claims to have been a party member. I find they have probative value and support the Appellant's assertion that he was a member of the HDP.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds HDP membership fee receipts valid and supportive of Appellant's membership claim.

propositions.text: Pir Sultan Abdal Cultural Association membership fees and card appear valid and support claim of Alevi Muslim identity
propositions.quote: The payments for membership fees and the membership card in the Pir Sultan Abdal Cultural Association appear valid, have probative value and support the Appellant's claim that he was an Alevi Muslim.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds membership fees and card for Pir Sultan Abdal Cultural Association valid and supportive of Alevi Muslim claim.

propositions.text: Letter from Canadian Alevi Culture Centre states Appellant is Alevi member since March 2017 but lacks detail on basis
propositions.quote: The letter from the Canadian Alevi Culture Centre, dated April 16, 2017, states that the Appellant is a member of the Alevi faith and had been a member of the community centre since March 2017. I note that the letter does not make clear how the Centre arrived at its finding that he was a member of the Alevi faith.

propositions.text: Assigns some probative value to the letter despite lack of detail
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, I assign the letter some probative value.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the letter states Appellant is Alevi member but lacks detail; assigns some probative value.

propositions.text: First three photographs said to be from Turkey protests show many people but no identifiable Appellant; no probative value
propositions.quote: The first three pictures said to be taken at protests in Turkey; however, they feature multiple people (as many as 40), none of whom appears to be the Appellant. I assign these no probative value.

propositions.text: Other three photos said to be from Canada have limited probative value as participation in Canada does not prove participation in Turkey
propositions.quote: The other three photographs are said to be taken at a time when the Appellant was here in Canada. Even accepting that these are pictures of the Appellant, they are of limited probative value. The fact that he has participated in Kurdish political events while in Canada does not prove that he did so in Turkey.

propositions.text: Appellant may have participated in Canada events to strengthen false refugee claim
propositions.quote: He may well have participated in the events in Canada with a view to strengthening a false refugee claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds first three photos show no Appellant and others have limited value; participation in Canada events may support false claim.

propositions.text: Weighing fraudulent behaviour against documents, finds Appellant overall lacks credibility
propositions.quote: When I weigh the Appellant's fraudulent behaviour, as outlined above, against to the documents outlined above and their probative value, I find that the Appellant is, overall, lacking in credibility.

propositions.text: Finds claims of persecution by Turkish state on HDP membership are false on balance of probabilities
propositions.quote: Consequently, I find that his claims of persecution by the Turkish state on the basis of his membership in the HDP are, on a balance of probabilities, false.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant lacks credibility and his claims of persecution due to HDP membership are false.

propositions.text: Considers whether someone similarly situated as Alevi Muslim in Turkey faces serious persecution or harm under IRPA
propositions.quote: it falls to me to consider whether someone similarly situated as a Alevi Muslim in Turkey would face a serious possibility of persecution or would face, on a balance of probabilities, harm of the nature outlined in subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court considers if a similarly situated Alevi Muslim in Turkey faces serious persecution or harm under IRPA.

propositions.text: Reviewed documents submitted to RPD including two about Alevi Muslims and National Documentation Package
propositions.quote: I have reviewed documents submitted by the Appellant before the RPD, only two of which touch on the situation of Alevi Muslims in Turkey, as well as the National Documentation Package.

propositions.text: Two articles submitted are of limited value: one from 1993 and one with passing reference to 2016 attack
propositions.quote: The two articles submitted by the Appellant before the RPD are of limited value: the first deals with an incident from 1993 and is not relevant to the situation in 2018 and the second makes only passing reference to a single incident involving an attack against Alevi neighbourhoods during the attempted coup in 2016.

paragraphs.summary: The court reviewed documents on Alevi Muslims, finding two articles of limited value due to age and limited relevance.

propositions.text: Alevi Muslims in Turkey face inequalities including lack of official recognition, worship difficulties, and religious instruction issues
propositions.quote: It is clear from the objective evidence that the 15 - 20 million Alevi Muslims in Turkey face inequalities. These include not having their places of worship officially recognized (and, therefore, not receiving financial support from the state), difficulties establishing new places of worship, a refusal to allow Alevi children an exemption from compulsory Sunni Islamic instruction; and an inability to state their religion on their identify cards (the government considers Alevism a heterodox Muslim sect).

propositions.text: Small number of ill-treatment reports mainly during demonstrations; isolated societal discrimination and violence reported but coexistence is common
propositions.quote: There have also been a small number of reports of ill-treatment of Alevis by the authorities, primarily in the context of demonstrations by the Alevi community. Isolated incidents of societal discrimination and violence towards Alevis have been reported but "these are few and most Alevis co-exist with other communities with few problems on a daily basis."

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Alevi Muslims face inequalities and some ill-treatment mainly during demonstrations but generally coexist peacefully.

propositions.text: UK Home Office summary states Alevi treatment does not amount to persecution or serious harm
propositions.quote: Even when taken cumulatively, the treatment faced by Alevis does not in general amount to them being subject to action on the part of either non-state actors or the authorities which would amount to persecution or serious harm.

propositions.text: Court agrees with UK Home Office summary that Alevi Muslims generally do not face serious persecution in Turkey
propositions.quote: I agree with this summary. I find that, despite the existence of problems, Alevi Muslims in general do not face a serious possibility of persecution in Turkey.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with UK Home Office that Alevi Muslims generally do not face serious persecution in Turkey.

propositions.text: Finds Appellant will not face serious persecution or harm under IRPA on return to Turkey
propositions.quote: Based the foregoing, I find the Appellant will not face a serious possibility of persecution on his return to Turkey. I find further that, on a balance of probabilities, he will not face harm of the nature described in subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant will not face serious persecution or harm under IRPA if returned to Turkey.

propositions.text: The Appeal is dismissed.
propositions.quote: The Appeal is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal.
